newsitem.title: USA: No need for new global forest pact - US's Wirth.
newsitem.headline: No need for new global forest pact - US's Wirth.

text.p: The United States does not believe a new international treaty is needed to achieve sustainable forestry management, Undersecretary of State for Global Affairs Tim Wirth said Wednesday.

In a speech to a forestry symposium, Wirth said there was no international consensus on key issues. It would be more useful, he said, to existing agreements and to focus work around several guiding principles.

Those principles would include elimination of government policies, such as subsidies and trade barriers, that discourage sustainable management, public participation in policy-setting, action to protect forest biodiversity and encouragement of responsible behavior by private landowners.
The U.N. General Assembly was scheduled to hold a special session in June on sustainable development, five years after the so-called Earth Summit in Rio de Janerio.
Some nations have called for a new international treaty to ensure high-priorty attention to forest preservation.
"The United States agrees that a holistic approach to forests is important, especially ata the national level in support of national priorities, but this does not require a new treaty," Wirth said.

To facilitate the idea that nations must be accountable for sustainable management of forests, Wirth suggested the convening of an Intergovernmental Forum on Forests under the U.N. Commisssion on Sustainable Development to report and review progress on implementation of items already agreed before the commission's Intergovernmental Panel on Forests.
The panel ended two years of discusson in February by endorsing 135 proposals for action to promote sustainable forest management worldwide.
